nodes.label: Copyright determinations
nodes.one_line: Make a defensible copyright call for copying or publishing archival material — unpublished status, duration, fair use — and record the reasoning.
know_what: Copyright — the exclusive bundle (17 U.S.C. §106: reproduce, distribute, display, perform, make derivatives) held by the author or rights holder, separate from physical ownership; the archive can hold the paper without holding the right

Unpublished status — U.S. works created before 1978 and never published were protected until the later of 70 years after the author's death or December 31, 2002 (and through 2047 if published by then); the biggest duration trap in archives holding letters and manuscripts
Publication — distribution of copies to the public (17 U.S.C. §101), which an archive triggers by putting images online; the act that switches duration and fair-use analysis
Duration — life of the author plus 70 years for post-1978 works; 95 years from publication or 120 from creation for works made for hire and anonymous or pseudonymous works

Fair use — 17 U.S.C. §107's four factors (purpose and character of use, nature of the work, amount and substantiality, effect on the market); the archive's main statutory route to serving unpublished material

Orphan works — works whose rights holder cannot be identified or located after a diligent search; the U.S. has no safe-harbor statute (unlike EU Directive 2012/28), so the archive documents the search instead of assuming clearance
First-sale doctrine — 17 U.S.C. §109 lets the archive lend and display the physical copies it owns, but authorizes neither copying nor digitization
Deed of gift — the acquisition document that can transfer or license copyright alongside physical custody; without an explicit grant, the right stays with the donor
Reasoned determination — the written analysis (status, duration, holder, fair-use factors) filed with the request; the artifact that makes a risky call defensible years later
Takedown policy — the notice-and-takedown procedure (17 U.S.C. §512 for online service providers) that bounds liability when the archive guesses wrong about a rights holder
know_how: Run the status-and-duration screen first: published or unpublished, pre-1978 or post-1978, named author with death date or anonymous — each answer changes the term
Determine publication status by the §101 test — was a copy distributed to the public — before applying any duration rule
Compute the term for a post-1978 authored work (life + 70) and for a work made for hire (95 from publication or 120 from creation) and state the end date in the determination
Apply the four fair-use factors to a copying or digitization request, writing one paragraph per factor with evidence — nature of the item, amount copied, market effect
Run the orphan-work diligence search — Copyright Office records, author registries, publisher and estate contacts — and log each step and date
Draft a deed-of-gift copyright clause that transfers or licenses the rights the archive needs for digitization and online access
File the reasoned determination with the request so a future staff member or a court can reconstruct the call
habits: Treat physical custody and copyright as two separate questions every time — 'we hold it' never answers 'may we publish it?'
Check publication status before duration; the classic error is assuming a letter is still protected because it is old, or public domain because it is unpublished
Write the determination before the scan, not after the takedown notice
When in doubt, document the doubt: name the unknown holder and the search steps rather than guessing
Keep the author's death date the way you keep the collection's box count — it drives every later call
nodes.checkpoint: Given five real requests to copy or publish archival items (a 1920s donor letter, a 1985 departmental report, an anonymous photograph from 1960, a 2008 email from a named author, a published 1941 pamphlet), write a reasoned copyright determination for each — status, duration, rights holder, fair-use factors where relevant — and get no error that a copyright librarian flags.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming old equals public domain, or 'the archive owns it so we can publish it': an unpublished 1923-1977 letter goes online without a determination and draws a takedown notice or a donor grievance. The mirror failure is over-restricting — refusing to serve or digitize everything because one item is risky, which quietly kills the access mission.
sources: U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 1 and Circular 22 (Copyright Basics; How to Investigate the Copyright Status of a Work)
Peter Hirtle, 'Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States' (Cornell Copyright Information Center)
Peter Hirtle, Emily Hudson, and Andrew Kenyon, Copyright and Cultural Institutions: Guidelines for Digitization for U.S. Libraries, Archives, and Museums (2009)

nodes.label: User studies
nodes.one_line: Run a small user study — log reference questions, track finding-aid success — and turn the findings into one description or access change.
know_what: User study — a small-scale, systematic look at who uses the archive and how, built from logs, surveys, or observation; distinct from anecdotal impressions at the reference desk
Reference-question log — the running record of every reference transaction — date, query, channel, series requested, outcome — the raw material of demand analysis
Finding-aid success tracking — measuring whether researchers navigate finding aids unaided: task completion, click paths, failed searches, staff interventions
Transaction analysis — the classic archival method of counting and categorizing reference questions over a period, converting the log into demand data
User population — researchers, students, genealogists, community members, journalists; each group's needs differ and the study must name its population
Success criteria — the pre-defined outcome (e.g., 'researcher locates the payroll series without staff help in under 10 minutes') that turns observation into pass or fail
Usability test — having a researcher attempt a defined task on the finding aid or catalog while staff observe and time them
Survey instrument — a short structured questionnaire (typically 10-15 questions) for exit interviews or remote users
Reference statistics — the compiled numbers (questions by type, retrievals, remote contacts) that justify staffing and digitization budgets
Change loop — the discipline of turning one study finding into one concrete change (a description edit, a finding-aid link, a policy tweak) and re-measuring
know_how: Keep a reference-question log for a defined period (e.g., one month), categorizing every question by topic, user type, and whether the finding aid got the researcher there
Run a transaction analysis: count questions by category, compute the share that required staff interpretation beyond the finding aid, and write a one-page summary
Set up a finding-aid usability test: one task per participant (find series X, locate dates for creator Y), timed, with the stuck point recorded
Design a 10-15 question exit survey for reading-room users and administer it for a week
Turn one finding into one change: revise a finding aid's scope note or add a series-level link, then re-test the same task
Write a short study report — population, method, results, one recommended change — under two pages
habits: Log the reference question at the desk, not from memory at the end of the week
Ask 'how did you find us?' in every interview — it is the cheapest usability data in the building
When a researcher gets lost in the finding aid, note where they got lost and fix that exact spot
Treat every repeated question as a description failure until proven otherwise
Re-run the same task after a change instead of assuming the fix worked
nodes.checkpoint: Run a four-week user study: log every reference transaction, categorize the questions, run one finding-aid usability task with five participants, and produce a two-page report with one recommended change that you then implement and re-test on the same task.
nodes.common_failure: Collecting statistics without a question: counting transactions for a year and having nothing to decide, or observing one frustrated researcher and 'fixing' the finding aid for them alone. The loop — log, analyze, change, re-measure — is the whole skill, and skipping any leg makes the study decorative.
sources: Paul Conway, 'Facts and Frameworks: An Approach to Studying the Users of Archives' (American Archivist, 1986)
Elizabeth Yakel, 'Thinking Inside and Outside the Box: Archival Reference Services at the Turn of the Century' (Archivaria, 2000)
Wendy Duff and Verne Harris, 'Stories and Names: Archival Description as Narrating Records and Constructing Meanings' (2002)
SAA, Reference and Access: Innovative Practices for Archives and Special Collections (2014)

nodes.label: Restrictions & privacy
nodes.one_line: Apply access restrictions — donor-imposed, statutory, privacy-based — to a request and cite the authority for denying or redacting, documenting the review.
know_what: Access restriction — a condition limiting who may see a record or what they may copy: donor-imposed, statutory, or privacy-based, each carrying a different authority and weight
Donor-imposed restriction — a term in the deed of gift ('closed until 2040', 'researcher must obtain family permission'); binding on the archive for the stated term
Statutory restriction — access limits set by law: FERPA for student records, HIPAA for health information, FOIA exemptions for government records, national security classifications
Privacy-based restriction — limits derived from the privacy interests of living persons named in records, applied by institutional policy where no statute covers the material
Redaction — copying a record with portions masked (names, medical details, third-party identities) so the rest can be served; distinct from denying the whole item
Authority citation — naming the specific legal or donor provision justifying a denial or redaction, so the decision can be audited
Review log — the documented record of each restriction decision: item, restriction applied, authority, staff member, date; the evidence that a denial was a procedure, not a whim
Deed of gift terms — the acquisition contract's access clauses; the archive's strongest defense when a donor's family challenges a decision later
Closure period — a fixed term (often 25, 50, or 75 years) after which a donor-imposed restriction lifts automatically
Privacy vs secrecy — the distinction between protecting identifiable living people and withholding material because it embarrasses an institution; the crux of the debate
know_how: Classify a restriction request into donor-imposed, statutory, or privacy-based and name the authority — deed clause, statute, or policy — for each
Cite the exact provision when denying or redacting ('closed under the deed of gift dated 1982, clause 4'; 'FERPA, 20 U.S.C. §1232g') rather than a personal judgment
Redact for third-party privacy: mask names and identifiers, keep the surrounding context, and note the redaction on the copy served
Calculate closure periods: from the deed or record date, state when the restriction lifts and make the finding aid say so
Document every review in the restriction log — item, restriction, authority, decision, date, reviewer — so a colleague can audit the call
Write the DACS access-restrictions note that tells researchers what is closed, why, and until when
Escalate a borderline call (privacy vs embarrassment) to the review procedure with the reasoning written down
habits: Ask 'whose authority?' for every restriction — no authority, no denial
Separate the person's privacy from the institution's embarrassment before applying any restriction
Redact rather than deny when a single name is the problem
Put the restriction in the finding aid so researchers know what they cannot see before they ask
Re-open files on schedule: closure periods end, and nobody re-checks them unless the calendar says so

know_why.claim: Restrictions — donor-imposed, statutory, and privacy-based — protect real people and legal interests, and an archive that applies them faithfully can still serve the record.
know_why.because: privacy-based and statutory restrictions prevent concrete harm to identifiable living people (health, student, personnel records), and the review log makes each denial auditable; the archive's legitimacy rests on the restriction being a cited procedure, never a staff judgment.
know_why.disputed_by: the community archives school argues restrictions in practice hide material: donor clauses let the powerful bury embarrassing history, and institutions stretch privacy rules to dodge accountability — so open access should be the default and any closure must be justified, time-limited, and controlled by the community the records are about rather than by the donor; access-first archivists share the suspicion of donor control while accepting statutory limits.
know_why.source: SAA, Reference and Access: Innovative Practices for Archives and Special Collections (2014); Menzi Behrnd-Klodt, Navigating Legal Issues in Archives (2008); Verne Harris, 'The Archival Sliver' (2002); the donor-restriction debate in American Archivist

nodes.checkpoint: Given six requested records (a personnel file, a 1980 donor letter with a closure clause, a medical record, an internal memo about a failed program, a student transcript, an unrestricted newsletter), decide serve, redact, or deny for each; cite the exact authority for every denial and redaction; and log each decision with date and reviewer in a review log a colleague can audit.
nodes.common_failure: Restricting from anxiety: closing or redacting everything with a living person's name, which denies access without a stated authority and collapses under the first challenge. The opposite failure is honoring donor clauses you never re-read — a 1982 deed's 'closed until 2000' gets forgotten and stays closed for decades because nobody scheduled the review.
sources: SAA, Reference and Access: Innovative Practices for Archives and Special Collections (2014)
Menzi Behrnd-Klodt, Navigating Legal Issues in Archives (SAA, 2008)
Heather MacNeil, Trusting Records: Legal, Historical and Diplomatic Perspectives (2000)
Verne Harris, 'The Archival Sliver: Power, Memory, and Archives in South Africa' (Archival Science, 2002)
FERPA (20 U.S.C. §1232g), HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR §164), and FOIA exemptions

nodes.label: Active records systems
nodes.one_line: Set up an office file plan — series folders, naming conventions, version control — so current records are findable without IT archaeology.
know_what: Active records — records in current use by the creating office, kept where staff work; the first stage of the lifecycle before retention and disposition
File plan — the office's agreed folder taxonomy, named by function or series, that every staff member uses for filing and retrieval
Records series — a group of records filed together under one system or produced by one activity; the unit a file plan names
Naming convention — the standard for folder and file names (e.g., YYYY-{series}-{descriptor}) that makes sort order meaningful and retrieval predictable
Version control — one canonical current version per document, with drafts and superseded versions kept or discarded per the file plan, never overwritten silently
Filing vs piling — placing a record in its planned location at creation or receipt versus letting it accumulate on the desk and in the inbox
Official record copy — the designated authoritative copy (usually the one filed in the recordkeeping system) versus convenience copies on the desktop
Shared drive hygiene — the network drive or team-site folder structure that mirrors the file plan instead of growing organically
Recordkeeping system — the software or physical arrangement designed to capture, maintain, and dispose of records by schedule
Metadata capture — the points (date, author, series) recorded at filing that make a file findable without opening it
know_how: Draft an office file plan: 5-10 series folders named by function, agreed with the office, with a written rule for where each new document goes
Design a naming convention (e.g., YYYYMMDD_series_short-description_vN) and test it against ten real files for sort order and uniqueness
Set up version control: one canonical file per document, a version stamp in the filename or metadata, and a rule for superseded drafts
Move an office's shared drive from a topic mess to the file plan, holding the top level to 5-10 folders
Write the one-page file-plan document — folders, naming rule, version rule, exceptions — that survives staff turnover
Run a retrieval test: pick ten random current records and time how long a colleague takes to find each under the new plan
habits: File at creation or receipt, not at 'cleanup day'
Name the series before the document: 'which folder does this belong to?' is the first filing question
Keep one canonical version; treat anything else as a dated draft
When a new document fits no folder, add a folder — never a miscellaneous pile
Ask 'would a stranger find this in my absence?' before closing a file
nodes.checkpoint: For a real office of 3-10 staff, produce a written file plan (5-10 function-based series folders), a naming convention that sorts correctly, and a version rule; move the shared drive or physical files to it; and show that a colleague can retrieve any of ten named current records in under two minutes each.
nodes.common_failure: Building the file plan on paper and stopping: the taxonomy is approved, nobody changes behavior, and the drive still grows a 'Misc' folder and twelve 'final_FINAL_v3' copies. A file plan not enforced at creation time is decoration — retrieval degrades back to search-and-hope within a quarter.
sources: ARMA International, Guidelines for File Plans and Records Retention
NARA, Managing Electronic Records and file-plan guidance
Jay Atherton, 'From Life Cycle to Continuum: Some Thoughts on the Records Management-Archives Relationship' (Archivaria, 1985-86)
ISO 15489-1:2016, Information and documentation — Records management

nodes.label: Records inventories
nodes.one_line: Run a records inventory — walk the office, list every series with volume and format — producing the data a retention schedule is built from.
know_what: Records inventory — the systematic survey of what an office holds: walking the space, listing every series with its volume, format, and location
Series-level capture — recording the inventory at the series level (not item level), naming each series and the function it serves
Volume measurement — counting in linear feet for paper (or boxes) and in gigabytes or file counts for electronic records, so the schedule can size the problem
Format identification — noting paper, photographs, microfilm, magnetic media, email, and databases, because each format carries different retention and preservation needs
Location register — the inventory's map of where each series lives: cabinet, shelf, drive path, database
Duplicate detection — flagging series that exist in multiple copies or multiple systems during the walk
Vital records — records essential to the office's continuity (charter, contracts, financials) that the inventory flags for protection
Inventory worksheet — the standard form (series name, function, volume, format, dates, location, owner) filled per series
Stakeholder interview — asking the office's staff where records live and what they mean before walking, because half the series sit in a cabinet nobody mentions
Completeness check — verifying the inventory against the office's functions and file plan so no series is missed
know_how: Prepare the walk: interview the office manager and two staff about where records live, then list the functions the records serve
Walk the office systematically — desks, cabinets, storage closets, shared drives, databases, email accounts — and fill one worksheet per series
Measure volume per series: linear feet for paper, gigabytes and file counts for electronic records
Record format and date ranges per series so the retention schedule can apply the right rules
Cross-check the inventory against the file plan and the office's function list, and chase every discrepancy
Flag duplicates, vital records, and records sitting in personal folders or home drives during the walk
Write the inventory summary: series count, total volume by format, and the five largest series by volume
habits: Interview before walking — staff know where the real records live
Count in the room, not from memory: open the cabinet, measure the shelf
List series by function, not by container ('legal correspondence', not 'cabinet 3')
Never trust the file plan alone — the walk exists to find the exceptions
Check the email and the shared drive even when the office says 'we have no electronic records'
nodes.checkpoint: For a real office, produce a complete records inventory: one worksheet per series with function, format, dates, and location; volume measured in linear feet or gigabytes; duplicates, vital records, and electronic records flagged; and a one-page summary listing the five largest series. A second person walking the same office must find no series the inventory missed.
nodes.common_failure: Inventorying the file room and missing the real records: the project correspondence lives in a project manager's desk drawer, the email lives on a shared mailbox, and the spreadsheet 'doesn't count'. A retention schedule built on a partial inventory authorizes the destruction of records the schedule never saw.
sources: NARA, Records Management Guidance and inventory worksheets
ARMA International, Records and Information Management Core Competencies
U.S. General Services Administration, Federal Records Management handbook
ISO 15489-1:2016, Information and documentation — Records management

nodes.label: Retention schedule authoring
nodes.one_line: Write a retention schedule for an office — every series, retention period, legal hold — so destruction is authorized and auditable, not accidental.
know_what: Retention schedule — the authoritative document assigning each series a retention period and disposition; the legal basis for destroying records
Series-to-period mapping — one line per series stating how long it is kept and what happens then: transfer, destroy, or retain permanently
Disposition — the authorized final action — transfer to archives, certified destruction, or permanent retention
Legal hold — a directive (litigation hold, investigation, FOIA request) that suspends destruction for named records until lifted; the schedule's most important override
Minimum retention — the floor set by statute or regulation (tax records 3-7 years, personnel records per state law) below which the office cannot schedule destruction
Schedule citation — the audit line (series, authority, retention, disposition) that makes each destruction defensible
Destruction certificate — the signed record of what was destroyed, when, and under which schedule line; the proof that destruction was authorized
Master vs office schedule — the institutional schedule covering all offices versus an office-specific one; offices inherit series from the master
Lifecycle trigger — the event that starts the clock (project close, employee departure, contract end) versus calendar-based retention from creation
Schedule approval — the sign-off chain (records manager, legal, agency head) that makes the schedule binding rather than a proposal
know_how: Turn the inventory into a schedule draft: one row per series with function, retention period, disposition, and the authority (statute, regulation, or business need) for the period
Distinguish calendar-based from event-based retention and state the trigger for each series
Research the statutory minimum for regulated series (tax, personnel, medical, contract) before proposing any period
Write the legal-hold clause: which records are suspended, by whose directive, and how the hold is lifted
Draft the destruction procedure the schedule points to: approval, certificate, and method (shredding, secure erase)
Circulate the draft for approval and record the approval dates so the schedule is legally binding
Set the review cycle (typically annual) for updating the schedule as functions change
habits: Schedule series, not documents — the unit of retention is the series
Ask 'what is the shortest defensible period?' instead of defaulting to 'keep forever'
Check the legal hold before every destruction, not as a footnote at the end
Cite the authority for every period — 'business need' alone does not survive an audit
Destroy on the calendar: a schedule that is never executed is a liability, because records kept past schedule stay discoverable
nodes.checkpoint: From a completed inventory, write a retention schedule for an office: one line per series with retention period, disposition, and cited authority; a legal-hold clause naming the suspended records and the directive; and a destruction procedure with certificate. A records manager must be able to execute any line without further research.
nodes.common_failure: Writing 'retain permanently' for everything because it feels safe: the schedule then authorizes nothing, the office keeps accumulating, or staff destroy on a guessed period and the first audit or lawsuit finds missing records. The schedule only works when every period carries an authority and the review cycle is real.
sources: NARA, General Records Schedules (GRS) and 'Records Management: Retention and Disposition'
ARMA International, Retention Management guidelines
Donald Skupsky, Recordkeeping Requirements (Information Requirements Clearinghouse)
ISO 15489-1:2016; ISO/TR 21946:2018, Information and documentation — Appraisal for managing records

nodes.label: Electronic records management
nodes.one_line: Tame a shared drive or ERM system — classification scheme, capture rules, disposal triggers — so digital records are managed in place instead of accumulating forever.
know_what: ERM system — an electronic records management system that classifies, captures, and disposes of records by schedule (SharePoint records management, OpenText, Alfresco, and similar)
Classification scheme — the ERM's file plan: the folder or metadata taxonomy every captured record is placed into
Capture rules — the automated or manual criteria deciding which documents become records to be captured ('all contracts', 'final versions only') versus transient material
Disposal triggers — the scheduled events (retention expiry, hold lift) that move records to archive or destruction inside the ERM
Shared drive — the unmanaged network folder structure where most born-digital records actually live; the ERM's main competitor
Metadata capture — the fields (series, date, author, classification) recorded at capture that make the record findable and schedulable
Declared record — the moment a document is formally declared a record and frozen against further editing
Journaling — automated capture of email and documents into the records system at the point of sending or saving
Hold mechanism — the ERM's way of suspending disposal for litigation or investigation
Scale problem — the volume reality (millions of files, thousands of users) that makes manual classification infeasible and forces automation or abandonment
know_how: Design the classification scheme for a shared drive or ERM: 5-10 top-level series from the file plan, applied to both folders and metadata
Write capture rules stating what gets captured (final contracts, approved policy) and what does not (drafts, personal files, junk)
Configure disposal triggers per series: retention expiry to archive or destroy, with legal holds overriding
Set up automatic metadata capture (author, date, series derived from the folder) so classification survives without staff effort
Run the declare-record workflow: final version declared, editing frozen, version history retained
Migrate a shared drive into the scheme — map old folders to new series, report the orphans — without losing records in transit
Test the disposal trigger on a sample series and verify the destruction log
habits: Capture at the moment of creation or receipt — 'file it or declare it now' — because backlogs never get classified
Assume the shared drive holds the real records until proven otherwise
When classification fails at volume, automate the metadata (folder-derived) instead of adding manual steps
Check holds before every disposal run, not after
Measure the system: capture rate, disposal rate, and the orphan-folder count are the ERM's health stats

know_why.claim: Capture-and-classify into an ERM or classified shared drive is the feasible way to manage born-digital records: automated metadata and capture rules let classification keep up with volume.
know_why.because: records left unclassified in place accumulate without retention or disposal, which is both a discovery liability and an archival loss, while folder-derived metadata and capture rules move the classification burden from people to the system.
know_why.disputed_by: the postcustodial school argues capture-and-classify fails at real volume — users will not classify, systems fall out of compliance, and the ERM becomes an empty shell while the shared drive holds the actual record — so stewardship should happen in place (distributed custody, description at creation, no forced capture), with the archive supervising rather than collecting; NARA's published reviews of failed ERM deployments are the evidence the school cites.
know_why.source: Frank Upward, 'Structuring the Records Continuum' (Archives and Manuscripts, 1996-97); NARA, 'Guidance on Managing Electronic Records' and ERM assessment reports; Kate Cumming, 'A Matter of Formalities: The Obstacles to Implementing Electronic Records Management' (2010)

nodes.checkpoint: For a shared drive with at least 5,000 files, build the classification scheme, write the capture rules, configure disposal triggers for three series with a legal hold on one, migrate the drive to the scheme with an orphan report, and demonstrate a test disposal that the hold blocks — with the system's capture rate logged.
nodes.common_failure: Buying the ERM and declaring victory: the system goes in, nobody declares records, the capture rate is near zero, and the shared drive keeps growing beside it — an empty shell costing licenses. The mirror failure is forcing manual classification on thousands of files, which staff abandon within a month and which leaves a drive classified by no one.
sources: NARA, 'Guidance on Managing Electronic Records' and ERM assessment reports
ISO 15489-1:2016; MoReq2010, Modular Requirements for Records Systems
Frank Upward, 'Structuring the Records Continuum' (Archives and Manuscripts, 1996-97)
Kate Cumming, 'A Matter of Formalities: The Obstacles to Implementing Electronic Records Management' (2010)
